Zero Replacement

Source: R/replace_zeros.r
replace_zeros.Rd

Replaces the zeros of a count table with small positive values, so that log ratios can be taken without a pseudocount. Runs any of ecodive's zero replacement methods by name, as count_ord() does for ordinations.

Usage

replace_zeros(counts, method, ...)

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of non-negative abundances (samples \(\times\) features), or any of the objects listed under Input Types. Counts or proportions.

method

The name of a zero replacement method: "mult", "czm", "gbm", "sq" or "bl". Flexible matching is supported (see below). Programmatic access via list_zero_replacements(). Required: there is no default, because the choice of method affects every downstream log ratio. "gbm" is the common choice for count tables (it is zCompositions' default).

...

Further arguments for the method's function, such as margin, replace_zeros_mult()'s delta, or frac, threshold and adjust (see replace_zeros_gbm()). Each method keeps its own defaults.

Value

The method's result: a dense numeric matrix of proportions with no zeros, in the orientation of counts (samples \(\times\) features for margin = 1, features \(\times\) samples for margin = 2), with its names. Each sample sums to 1. Attributes method (the method's id), then the method's results, ending with n_replaced, the number of zeros replaced. replace_zeros(counts, 'gbm', ...) is the same as replace_zeros_gbm(counts, ...).

Details

Logs of zero are undefined, so every log-ratio method, such as norm = 'clr', aitchison(), alr() and ilr(), needs the zeros dealt with. A pseudocount added to every value changes the ratios between the non-zero parts, and acts as an arbitrary weighting. A zero replacement instead gives each zero a small value and scales the sample's non-zero parts down to make room for it, keeping their ratios.

The result has no zeros, so it can be given to any of those functions without a pseudocount (and without the warning that pseudocount = NULL gives for zeros). The result is in proportions: every log-ratio method is scale invariant, so nothing is lost.

mult gives every zero the same proportion, whatever the sample's depth. The other methods are for counts: czm imputes a fraction of one read in each sample, and the Bayesian-multiplicative methods (gbm, sq, bl) also use how abundant the feature is in the other samples. gbm is the common default for count tables.

Conclusions that depend on how zeros were treated are fragile. Repeating an analysis with each method of list_zero_replacements('id') is a simple check.

List of Zero Replacement Methods

Option / Function NameMethod Name
multMultiplicative replacement, with a fixed value \(\delta\) (replace_zeros_mult())
czmCount zero multiplicative (replace_zeros_czm())
gbmGeometric Bayesian-multiplicative (replace_zeros_gbm())
sqSquare-root Bayesian-multiplicative (replace_zeros_sq())
blBayes-Laplace Bayesian-multiplicative (replace_zeros_bl())

Flexible name matching

Case insensitive and partial matching, ignoring anything but letters. E.g. method = 'MULT', 'multiplicative' or 'multiplicative replacement' selects mult, and 'GBM' or 'geometric Bayesian-multiplicative' selects gbm. Common other names also work: 'multRepl' (from zCompositions) and 'multi_replace' (from scikit-bio) for mult; 'cmultRepl' (zCompositions' function, whose default method is GBM) for gbm; 'square root' for sq; and 'Laplace' for bl.

Finished code should always use the full primary option name to avoid ambiguity with future additions to the list of methods.

Same names in other packages

None known. zCompositions' multRepl() and cmultRepl(), and scikit-bio's multi_replace(), do the same job under other names.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

References

Martín-Fernández, J. A., Barceló-Vidal, C., & Pawlowsky-Glahn, V. (2003). Dealing with zeros and missing values in compositional data sets using nonparametric imputation. Mathematical Geology, 35, 253–278. doi:10.1023/A:1023866030544

Martín-Fernández, J. A., Hron, K., Templ, M., Filzmoser, P., & Palarea-Albaladejo, J. (2015). Bayesian-multiplicative treatment of count zeros in compositional data sets. Statistical Modelling, 15, 134–158. doi:10.1177/1471082X14535524

Lubbe, S., Filzmoser, P., & Templ, M. (2021). Comparison of zero replacement strategies for compositional data with large numbers of zeros. Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems, 210, 104248. doi:10.1016/j.chemolab.2021.104248

See also

replace_zeros_mult(), replace_zeros_gbm(), list_zero_replacements(); aitchison(), alr(), ilr() and normalize() ('clr'), which take the result.

Examples

    x <- replace_zeros(ex_counts, 'gbm')
    x[1:3, 1:4]
#>        Streptococcus Bacteroides Corynebacterium Haemophilus
#> Saliva    0.46872444 0.005786721     0.001056911 0.520804933
#> Gums      0.89408789 0.004509901     0.001056911 0.098090349
#> Nose      0.02176063 0.001978239     0.492581602 0.001978239
    attr(x, 'n_replaced')
#> [1] 4

    # No zeros left, so no pseudocount is needed.
    aitchison(x)
#> # A dist: 4 samples (lower triangle)
#> # Aitchison Distance
#>       Saliva  Gums Nose
#> Gums    1.95
#> Nose   11.2  10.6
#> Stool   9.36  9.09 10.4
#> # Attributes: method

    # The same analysis with every method.
    lapply(list_zero_replacements('id'), function (m) {
      aitchison(replace_zeros(ex_counts, m))
    })
#> [[1]]
#> # A dist: 4 samples (lower triangle)
#> # Aitchison Distance
#>       Saliva  Gums Nose
#> Gums    3.12
#> Nose    8.58  9.54
